content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem's symptom line: the shop held far more purchases for fraud review. I'm aiming for a short, active sentence with no specific number, and I'm settling on something like "The shop held many more purchases for fraud review."

Next I'm working out the causal chain for the postmortem: the one replica that started on an A100 card at onset while the others run V100, and why deploys, flag changes, and mid-rollout states don't account for it.

I'm now checking the postmortem's numbers against the sources, so the figures stay consistent. Next I'm working out the third step of the causal chain: the fraud scorer on the A100 card and why it would decide differently from the V100 replicas.

I'm now writing the third step of the chain: the fraud scorer on the A100 card rounds its operands to TF32, which the code allows on that card, so its scores and hold decisions come out different from the V100 replicas.

I'm now writing the root-cause step: the fraud logit comes from a small gap between two large, nearly cancelling products, and the scorer rounds those operands to TF32 on the A100, so the rounding error swamps the gap and the hold decisions become mostly noise. I'm still treating that mechanism as unverified, since it rests on code I haven't run.

I'm wording the postmortem's root-cause description in plain terms: one copy of the service started on a different kind of graphics card than the others, and the fraud check probably rounds its numbers more coarsely there, enough to change its decisions and hold more purchases for review. I'm also drafting the risk note, that any replica placed on an A100 card could again hold far more purchases than its peers if the V100 hold is lifted.

I'm now weighing the contributing factors: the scheduler let the io-shop pods land on mixed accelerator types, since nothing held them to a single card before the incident. That is what let a replica end up on an A100 at all. The mitigation of holding the pods to V100 cards already addresses it, though turning sync back on would undo that.

I'm settling the second contributing factor: no test checked that the fraud model makes the same decisions on every accelerator type, and the test file says the Ampere behaviour was deliberately left untested. I'm planning to propose a cross-accelerator consistency check for every model scoring path.

I'm weighing the third contributing factor: nobody was paged, since the alert fired but no on-call incident was linked. Paging someone wouldn't have shortened this one, though, since Argus mitigated it quickly, so I'm treating it as a finding rather than a cause.

I'm settling the postmortem's alert point: the FraudHoldsHigh alert paged nobody, since no on-call incident was linked to it. I'm also considering whether the shop-wide average hid the spike from view, so the detection gap may belong with the contributing factors.

I'm listing the action items for the postmortem: first, writing the io-shop pods' hold to V100 cards into the repository so that turning automatic sync back on keeps it in place. Next I'm planning a check that runs the fraud scorer's decisions on every accelerator type.

I'm now listing the action items: writing a constraint into the repository that holds io-shop's pods to V100 cards, so turning sync back on keeps it. I'm also planning a check that runs the fraud scorer's decisions on every accelerator type the cluster can schedule io-shop onto, failing on any disagreement. For the detection side, I'm noting that FraudHoldsHigh should be linked to an on-call rotation so it pages someone.

Now I'm checking which parts of the incident record the postmortem can state as fact: the replica that started on an A100 at onset, Argus reading the flag history and ruling flags out, and the Mitigation Agent holding the pods to V100 cards as a reversible step. I'm also noting that the Code-Fix Agent's draft PR #534 is proposed but not something I'll describe here. Next I'm weighing what nobody being paged means for the went-wrong list, and whether the one diverging replica among three is worth calling out as luck.

I'm settling the scope of the rise: only the replica started at onset landed on an A100 card, while the others stayed on V100 cards, so I'm reasoning that the extra holds were confined to what that replica scored. I'm treating that as an inference from the shop-wide series, since I haven't read the per-replica hold shares.

I'm now fixing the wording of the causal chain's onset step: as the replica read at that point, the one started on an A100 card while the other replicas stayed on V100 cards, so I'll state that plainly and keep the replica's name exactly as recorded.

Next I'm wording the fourth step of the chain: on the A100 card the scorer likely rounds the fraud model's inputs and weights to TF32, which would change its hold decisions. Then I'm moving on to the went-wrong list.

I'm going to finish the postmortem's "went well" and "got lucky" lists, then move on to the assumptions.

action_items.item: Write the constraint holding io-shop's pods to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards into the service's repository, so that turning automatic sync back on keeps it rather than undoing it.
Add a check, run on every change to io-shop's scoring code, that compares the fraud scorer's decisions on each card type io-shop can be scheduled onto and fails on any disagreement.
Link the FraudHoldsHigh alert to an on-call rotation so that it pages a person when it fires.

causal_chain.step: The shop held a much larger share of purchases for fraud review than before the onset, enough to fire FraudHoldsHigh. Failed requests did not rise.

ruled_out.what: A deploy, release or flag change on the service in the day before the onset: the change events read back none.
A flag change by anyone but Argus in the hour before {T13.4}: the flag provider's history showed none.
A rollout caught partway through: all {T10.2} replicas ran one revision.

causal_chain.step: As read at {T7.1}, the replica io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p had started at the onset on an NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB card. The other replicas ran on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards.
Running the fraud scorer on the A100 card raised the share of purchases held. Once every pod was held to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards, the service was no longer at the incident's level from {T18.2}.
On the A100 card, the scorer in the files Code-Fix read rounds the fraud model's weights and inputs to TF32, which changes its hold decisions.

input.cause_in_plain_words: One copy of the shop's service started on a different kind of graphics card from the others, and on that card the fraud check likely rounds its numbers coarsely enough to change its decisions, so it held many more purchases for review.

contributing_factors.factor: Before the incident, io-shop's pods were held to no card type, so the scheduler could put a replica on an A100 card next to replicas on V100 cards.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Had the pods been held to one card type, the replica started at the onset would not have landed on an A100 card, and the scorer would have kept making the same decisions on every replica.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that the fraud scorer makes the same decisions on every card type it can run on. The test file's docstring said Ampere behaviour was deliberately left untested.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test comparing A100 decisions with V100 decisions would have shown the TF32 divergence before any replica scored real purchases on an A100.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

got_lucky: Only the replica started at the onset landed on an A100 card. The others stayed on V100 cards, so the rise was confined to the purchases that one replica scored.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent recorded where each replica runs, which showed that the replica started at the onset was the only one on an A100 card.
Argus read the flag provider's history and found no flag changes by anyone else, which ruled flags out alongside the empty deploy history.
The Mitigation Agent held io-shop's pods to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards, an action that can be put back.
The Mitigation Agent checked the service and confirmed the action, finding the service no longer at the incident's level.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #534.

went_wrong: The FraudHoldsHigh alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.

input.root_cause: The fraud model's logit is the small difference between two large products of opposite sign (weights of {F1.1} and {F1.2}). In src/io_shop/fraud_scoring.py, `fraud_logit` rounds every operand to TF32, which keeps only {F1.3} significand bits, whenever `ALLOW_TF32` is True and the card is listed in `TF32_ACCELERATORS`, and that list holds NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB. On an A100 the rounding changes each product by more than the difference the decision depends on, so the logit there, and with it the hold decision, is mostly rounding error.
input.still_at_risk: Any replica of the shop that lands on an A100 card again, once its pods are no longer held to V100 cards, could again hold far more purchases for review than its peers.
input.symptom: The shop held far more purchases for fraud review than usual
